segments.line: Day seven, the lights go out.
People who have studied a world without humans think most power stations would shut down within hours.
Nobody is left to balance the grid. Your city was
lucky. Its power comes from a dam in the mountains, and a dam can keep spinning on its own for weeks.
Until something, somewhere, trips. You're on the hotel
roof when it happens. One district goes dark, then the next, then
the whole skyline, until the only light left is the moon. A
few hours later, your phone drops to no signal. Phone
masts have backup batteries, and most of them only last a few hours. Then
the water. Under the streets, the subway starts to flood. New York's subway pumps out about
thirteen million gallons of water every single day.
Without the pumps, its own engineers thought parts of it could flood in about thirty- six hours. That's real. Then
the food. Without fridges, the fresh food in every supermarket rots within days. You
smell the meat counter from the car park.
Canned food lasts for years. If you can find a can opener. Then
the fuel. Petrol starts to go stale after about three to six months. After that,
every car in the city is just a very heavy chair. And then
the scary one. There are more than four hundred nuclear reactors on Earth. Without people, they
shut themselves down. But their fuel stays hot for years, and it has to be cooled. When
the power goes, backup diesel generators keep the cooling running. In
the United States, they must carry fuel for about seven days.
After that, nobody is there to refill them. You
count on your fingers. Today is day eight.
